passage:
My name is Simran, and I live next door to Maria's parents. I only know what I saw over the wall on Sunday.

Maria's mother had been telling everyone at the temple that Maria was about to be made a manager. That evening Maria arrived, still in her work shoes, and sat down at the table under the veranda light. Her parents stopped talking when she came in.

I couldn't hear all of it, but I heard Maria say, "I didn't get it. Someone else did. I should have told you last week." Her father stared at his tea. Her mother reached over and held Maria's wrist for a moment.

Later the mother came to water the plants, humming. I don't know how she really felt. But Maria was laughing at something by the time I went inside.

qa.q: Where did Simran see Maria sit with her parents?
qa.a: Simran saw Maria sit at the table under the veranda light.

qa.q: What does the mother's touch on Maria's wrist suggest, and how sure can Simran be?
qa.a: Holding Maria's wrist suggests warmth and support, but Simran admits not knowing how the mother really felt, so the inner state is uncertain.

qa.q: What did Maria do that helped with the awkwardness?
qa.a: Maria told her parents plainly that she did not get the role and that she should have said so sooner, instead of letting them hear it from others.

qa.q: How might the parents have felt after telling relatives that Maria was rising?
qa.a: They may have felt awkward or embarrassed in front of the relatives, though their quiet reaction and the later humming suggest they were not blaming Maria.

grounding: Parents had told relatives Maria was rising; a neighbour watches Maria tell them plainly about the setback and the family stay close.

passage: Ayesha, you look like you've swallowed a stone. Your parents told the whole family you'd be made manager, and now you weren't. I know that face. At your age, twenty-five, I was at the insurance office in Lucknow, and my Abbu had told every uncle at Eid that his daughter would be branch head. Then they gave it to someone else. I hid in the washroom at work, ashamed, because I'd let him down in front of everyone. For two weeks I dodged his calls. Finally I went home and said it straight: "Abbu, I didn't get it. The other person had more experience. I'll try again next year." He was quiet for a moment. Then he said, "You think I'm proud of a title? I'm proud of you." I cried into my tea. And I got it two years later. Your Salma-khala knows how this feels.

qa.q: What had Salma's Abbu told every uncle at Eid?
qa.a: That his daughter would be branch head.

qa.q: What did Salma feel when she didn't get the post?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and embarrassed, hiding in the washroom because she believed she had let her father down in front of everyone.

qa.q: What turning point helped Salma in the story?
qa.a: Going home and telling her Abbu plainly what happened, instead of dodging his calls for longer.

qa.q: How might Salma's Abbu have felt about telling the uncles?
qa.a: He may have felt awkward at first, but his words show he cared more about his daughter than the title.

grounding: An elder recalls being passed over after her father boasted to relatives; she felt ashamed, told him plainly, and learned her worth was not her title.

passage:
The wedding band was so loud in the Ludhiana marriage hall that Himani had to lean close to her father's ear. Every cousin had asked her the same question since dinner: "So, you're a senior associate now?" Papa had told them all, months ago, that it was certain.
It wasn't. The letter came on Monday. Somebody else.
"Papa, can we step outside?"
In the car park, away from the dhol, her face burned. "I didn't get the promotion. I'm sorry you told everyone. I should have told you on Monday."
Papa rubbed his forehead. Her brother Pranav, who had followed them out, said quickly, "It's one year, Himani. You'll get it."
Papa nodded slowly. "I was showing off. That's my embarrassment, not yours. What happened?"
She told him: a stronger candidate, a review in March. He squeezed her shoulder, and they went back in to dance.

qa.q: Where did Himani tell her father about the promotion?
qa.a: In the car park outside the Ludhiana marriage hall, away from the dhol.

qa.q: Why did Himani's face burn in the car park?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and embarrassed for letting her father down after he had told all the relatives the promotion was certain.

qa.q: How did Himani handle her father's pride in front of the family?
qa.a: She stepped outside and told him plainly what had happened, including the stronger candidate and the March review.

qa.q: How might Papa see the situation after hearing the truth?
qa.a: Papa feels embarrassed at his own boasting, but he recognises it as his feeling, not Himani's failure, and supports her.

grounding: The protagonist feels ashamed that her parent boasted of her rise; she tells him plainly what happened and learns the setback does not change her worth to him.
